They were actually meant to signal legitimacy to large-company buyers in targeted areas, reducing concerns that Airtable was an unknown startup when those buyers sought six-figure budgets. sections.heading: What critics saw—and what the billboards were for
sections.content: Critics on Twitter objected that the billboards were not specific to a particular problem and seemed to make no sense. Egner said their real purpose was not to explain a product use case: Airtable wanted to signal to large companies that it was established and trustworthy. The team targeted areas where fashion and media companies had offices, reasoning that employees who saw a billboard on the way to work might be more receptive when later asking IT for a six-figure Airtable budget, rather than seeing Airtable as an unfamiliar startup.

sections.heading: How they made the tactic practical
sections.content: Airtable mostly bought remnant billboard inventory—less desirable placements left near the end of a buying cycle—which could be cheap while still being in the desired area. Egner described this as a way to reduce the risk of losing deals because the company seemed too small. She said some inventory could cost in the low thousands, depending on the metro, and noted the billboards were useful but not among the company’s highest-ROI tactics.

sections.heading: What critics saw—and what Airtable intended
sections.content: Critics on Twitter questioned why Airtable was running billboards that did not focus on a specific problem and seemed unclear. Egner said the actual goal was not the message critics expected: to signal to large companies that Airtable was established and trustworthy. The team placed billboards near offices of target companies in New York’s fashion and media industries, so employees might recognize the brand when seeking IT approval for a six-figure Airtable budget. That familiarity could make Airtable seem less like an unknown startup and reduce the risk of losing deals because the company was small.

sections.heading: How they kept it affordable
sections.content: Airtable mostly bought remnant inventory—unsold billboard placements near the end of a buying cycle—which could still be in desired locations at lower prices. Egner said some such inventory could cost in the low thousands of dollars, though prices varied widely by metro; she described the billboards as useful, but not the company’s highest-ROI tactic.
